title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
義而教天下之忠也夫然後為諸侯者覩王制
之聿新大明乎靖恭之節思王章之有恪共輸
其精白之忱禮行於朝而愛心生焉所以媚茲
一人者真知其情之有不可解而莫不來享莫
不來王合同姓異姓而皆然矣何侯度之不明
也哉禮行於覲而敬心生焉所以欽若從王者
真見於分之有不可逃而以考制度以明黜陟
合大邦小邦而同然矣何臣紀之或昧也哉謂
之曰知所以臣信乎天王彰紀法之宗而百辟
===
遵紀法之守以行於一時則一時知所以臣也
以行於萬世則萬世知所以臣也武王復古禮
而教臣忠如此周道其極隆矣乎抑天下勢而
已矣勢之所在禮由出焉聖王壹戎衣有天下
勢已定矣而不以禮維之亂未巳也故禮射脫
劒明堂朝覲之教不憚其煩正以消其悖戾而
使之常定也然論勢則朝廷為重正體統尊朝
廷吾於朝覲有厚望焉
第貳場
punctuated:
義，而教天下之忠也。夫然後為諸侯者，覩王制之聿新，大明乎靖恭之節；思王章之有恪，共輸其精白之忱。禮行於朝而愛心生焉，所以媚茲一人者，真知其情之有不可解，而「莫不來享，莫不來王」，合同姓、異姓而皆然矣，何侯度之不明也哉？禮行於覲而敬心生焉，所以欽若從王者，真見於分之有不可逃，而以考制度、以明黜陟，合大邦、小邦而同然矣，何臣紀之或昧也哉？謂之曰「知所以臣」，信乎天王彰紀法之宗，而百辟遵紀法之守。以行於一時，則一時知所以臣也；以行於萬世，則萬世知所以臣也。武王復古禮而教臣忠如此，周道其極隆矣乎！抑天下勢而已矣，勢之所在，禮由出焉。聖王壹戎衣有天下，勢已定矣，而不以禮維之，亂未巳也。故禮射、脫劒、明堂、朝覲之教，不憚其煩，正以消其悖戾，而使之常定也。然論勢則朝廷為重，正體統、尊朝廷，吾於朝覲有厚望焉。

第貳場
translation_en:
… duty, and teaches loyalty to all under Heaven. Only after this did the feudal lords, beholding the renewal of royal institutions, gain a great understanding of the integrity of quiet reverence; and reflecting on the solemnity of the royal statutes, together offer up their pure and unblemished sincerity. When ritual is practiced at the spring court audience (chao), feelings of affection arise therein. Those who thus show devotion to the One Man truly know that their bond of affection cannot be severed, so that "there is none who does not come to make offerings, none who does not come to acknowledge the king's sovereignty"—uniting lords of the same surname and of different surnames alike in this. How could the regulations for feudal lords not be clear? When ritual is practiced at the autumn audience (jin), feelings of reverence arise therein. Those who thus reverently obey and follow the king truly see that their allotted duty cannot be escaped, and through the examination of institutions and the clarification of promotions and demotions, great states and small states alike are united in this. How could the discipline of ministers ever be obscured? To say that they "knew how to act as subjects"—truly, the Heavenly King manifested the foundation of rules and laws, and the hundred lords abided by the observance of those rules and laws! Put into practice for a single age, that single age knows how to act as subjects; put into practice for ten thousand generations, ten thousand generations know how to act as subjects. King Wu restored the ancient rituals and taught his ministers loyalty in this manner—how supremely flourishing was the Way of Zhou! Yet all under Heaven is a matter of the configuration of power (shi) and nothing more; where power resides, ritual emerges therefrom. Once the sage king donned armor to take possession of all under Heaven, the configuration of power was already settled; yet if he had not maintained it through ritual, disorder would not have ceased. Therefore, he did not shrink from the trouble of instituting the teachings of ritual archery, unbuckling swords, the Hall of Distinction (Mingtang), and the spring and autumn court audiences, precisely so as to dissolve perversity and rebelliousness and keep the realm constantly settled. Yet in discussing the configuration of power, the royal court is paramount; for rectifying the system of hierarchy and honoring the court, I place high hopes in the spring and autumn audiences.

Second Session

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
論
人主當防未萌之欲
朱用光
同考試官教諭田批作此題者只是說防欲不
會發得未萌之欲此作窮徹本原矣
同考試官教諭畢批作論者多喜馳騁浮語惟
此全在心上作工夫深得題旨
考試官教諭林批說理之文
考試官教諭吳批理邃詞逸
===
無欲者其心之初乎人君察其幾而防之豫則
心之天常如初而欲不能爲之累矣夫人主一
心萬事萬化取則焉一旦而或動于欲常患其
不知防知防矣則其端雖萌終必隱伏而不得
肆夫有欲而使其不得肆是亦足矣而不知此
心之天其初未始有欲也凡欲者皆人也非天
也後來之所交引而非其初之本有也夫欲非
此心之初而必待其旣有而後求其無其時亦
已晚而其力亦已難矣人主思端運化之本而
punctuated:
論

人主當防未萌之欲

朱用光
同考試官教諭田批：作此題者，只是說防欲，不會發得未萌之欲。此作窮徹本原矣。
同考試官教諭畢批：作論者多喜馳騁浮語，惟此全在心上作工夫，深得題旨。
考試官教諭林批：說理之文。
考試官教諭吳批：理邃詞逸。

無欲者，其心之初乎！人君察其幾而防之豫，則心之天常如初，而欲不能爲之累矣。夫人主一心，萬事萬化取則焉。一旦而或動于欲，常患其不知防；知防矣，則其端雖萌，終必隱伏而不得肆。夫有欲而使其不得肆，是亦足矣，而不知此心之天，其初未始有欲也。凡欲者，皆人也，非天也；後來之所交引，而非其初之本有也。夫欲非此心之初，而必待其旣有而後求其無，其時亦已晚，而其力亦已難矣。人主思端運化之本，而
translation_en:
Discourse

"A Ruler Ought to Guard Against Desires Before They Sprout"

By Zhu Yongguang 朱用光
Associate Examiner and Instructor Tian comments: Those who write on this topic merely speak of guarding against desires, failing to bring out the meaning of desires "before they sprout." This piece has thoroughly penetrated to the fundamental source.
Associate Examiner and Instructor Bi comments: Writers of discourses mostly like to indulge in unrestrained, superficial verbiage; this piece alone concentrates entirely on working upon the mind, deeply grasping the purport of the topic.
Examiner and Instructor Lin comments: An essay that expounds moral principle.
Examiner and Instructor Wu comments: Profound in principle and transcendent in phrasing.

To be without desire—is that not the original state of the mind! If a ruler discerns its subtle incipient stirrings and guards against them beforehand, then the heavenly nature of his mind will always remain as it was at the beginning, and desires will not be able to encumber it. Now the single mind of the ruler is that from which the myriad affairs and myriad transformations take their model. Should it once be moved by desire, the constant worry is that he does not know how to guard against it; yet if he does know how to guard against it, then even though its beginnings may sprout, in the end they must lie hidden and be unable to run rampant. Now to have desires and yet keep them from running rampant would seem sufficient; however, one fails to realize that in the heavenly nature of this mind, at the beginning there were never any desires at all. All desires are of human artifice, not of Heaven; they are drawn forth by subsequent interactions with external things, and are not originally inherent in the mind's initial state. Since desire is not part of the original state of this mind, if one must wait until it already exists before seeking to eliminate it, the timing is already late and the effort required is already difficult. When a ruler reflects upon making upright the foundation that guides transformation, and yet…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
顧任其晚且難無論不識不力雖識與力無救
於害也是故人主欲保其本然之天其必及其
初而豫防其人乎初者欲未萌之時也豫之云
者防於未萌之謂也而因以是申程氏之說夫
以天下之大萬幾之煩惟人主所裁制而以有
欲之心主宰於其間則天下始有不得其理者
故人主不可有欲也而欲實爲人主所恒有夫
惟其欲之恒有也禁之則止縱之則熾止則階
福熾則速戾其辨甚著也故欲不可不防也而
===
昔人之言防者大端有二有防於已萌者太甲
之圖厥終秦誓之憂逾邁是也有防於未萌者
禮之禁未發詩之保無射是也其防則一而遲
疾難易之效判然殊焉何以明其然也蓋齊民
之欲難遂而人主之欲易窮衆庶之欲易節而
人主之欲難制玉帛萬國奔走遐方任土作貢
畢獻方物其欲之萌罔弗得也巧嬖諧媚伺便
頤指齒馬投鼠莫敢先事其欲之萌罔以禁也
以易窮之資挾難制之勢而恣其已萌之欲卽
punctuated: 顧任其晚且難，無論不識不力，雖識與力，無救於害也。是故人主欲保其本然之天，其必及其初而豫防其人乎！初者，欲未萌之時也；豫之云者，防於未萌之謂也。而因以是申程氏之說。夫以天下之大、萬幾之煩，惟人主所裁制，而以有欲之心主宰於其間，則天下始有不得其理者。故人主不可有欲也，而欲實爲人主所恒有。夫惟其欲之恒有也，禁之則止，縱之則熾；止則階福，熾則速戾，其辨甚著也。故欲不可不防也。而昔人之言防者，大端有二：有防於已萌者，《太甲》之「圖厥終」、《秦誓》之「憂逾邁」是也；有防於未萌者，《禮》之「禁未發」、《詩》之「保無射」是也。其防則一，而遲疾難易之效判然殊焉。何以明其然也？蓋齊民之欲難遂，而人主之欲易窮；衆庶之欲易節，而人主之欲難制。玉帛萬國，奔走遐方，任土作貢，畢獻方物，其欲之萌，罔弗得也；巧嬖諧媚，伺便頤指，齒馬投鼠，莫敢先事，其欲之萌，罔以禁也。以易窮之資，挾難制之勢，而恣其已萌之欲，卽
translation_en:
…yet instead leaves it until it is late and difficult—not to mention lacking the awareness or the strength, even with awareness and strength, there will be no saving it from harm. Therefore, if a ruler wishes to preserve his inherent Heavenly nature, must he not take advantage of its initial state and take precautions against human artifice beforehand? The "initial state" refers to the time when desires have not yet sprouted; "taking precautions beforehand" means guarding against them before they have sprouted. And from this, we may elaborate upon Master Cheng's doctrine.

Now, given the vastness of the empire and the myriad complexities of state affairs, all are decided and regulated solely by the ruler. If a mind harbouring desires presides over them, then things throughout the empire will begin to lose their proper order. Therefore, a ruler must not have desires—and yet desires are in fact something rulers constantly have. Precisely because desires are constantly present, if one restrains them, they cease; if one indulges them, they blaze forth. When they cease, it leads to blessing; when they blaze forth, it invites calamity—the distinction is crystal clear. Thus, one cannot fail to guard against desires.

In antiquity, those who spoke of guarding against them generally fell into two categories. There were those who guarded against desires after they had already sprouted—such as "planning for the end" in the Taijia (Tai Jia) and "worrying over the passing of time" in the Qinshi (Oath of Qin). And there were those who guarded against desires before they had sprouted—such as "prohibiting before it arises" in the Record of Rites (Li) and "preserving without weariness" in the Odes (Shi). The act of guarding is the same, yet the effects in terms of earliness or lateness, ease or difficulty, are starkly different. How can we explain why this is so?

The desires of commoners are hard to satisfy, whereas the desires of a ruler are easily indulged to the utmost; the desires of the multitude are easily moderated, whereas the desires of a ruler are hard to restrain. With jade and silk from ten thousand states and distant regions hastening to serve, offering tribute according to local products and presenting all manner of regional goods, whenever a desire of his sprouts, there is nothing he cannot obtain. With artful favourites flattering and fawning, watching for the slightest nod of his chin to do his bidding, and with courtiers as fearful of offending as one who shrinks from inspecting the teeth of the ruler's horse or throwing at a rat near a precious vessel, so that none dares to forestall the matter, whenever a desire of his sprouts, there is no way to prohibit it. Relying on resources that easily allow indulgence to the utmost, backed by an authority that is hard to restrain, if he gives free rein to desires that have already sprouted, even if…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
幸而明諸心矣未必遽防也即防矣未必能遽
復也即復矣而未復之前其害弗可極亦弗可
追也蓋防於已萌者其效如此則初之不豫之
過也復其本然之天而非保其本然之天也是
故善防欲者不當防於已萌之後而當防於未
萌之先夫未萌之先本然之天也心之初也其
猶鑑之明而水之清乎鑑欲其常明時其未蔽
而拂拭之則塵垢不止而妍媸常定矣水欲其
常清時其未淆而正錯之則湛濁不動足以燭
===
鬚眉而察理矣君心之天其初而欲之未萌也
虛然明耳湛然清耳當是之時有理無欲有天
無人完其理守其天而不以人欲參焉其爲防
甚易也然而理與欲迭爲貞勝天與人迭爲消
長故出乎理則入乎欲人爲主則天必漓自此
則牽引蔓延潰裂四出而始難防矣非防之難
其防於已萌者之難也若夫未萌之防則人主
之所以易其防也是衆人以爲不必防而君子
深以爲當防者也知其當防及其初而豫爲之
punctuated: 幸而明諸心矣，未必遽防也；即防矣，未必能遽復也；即復矣，而未復之前，其害弗可極，亦弗可追也。蓋防於已萌者，其效如此，則初之不豫之過也，復其本然之天，而非保其本然之天也。是故善防欲者，不當防於已萌之後，而當防於未萌之先。夫未萌之先，本然之天也，心之初也，其猶鑑之明而水之清乎！鑑欲其常明，時其未蔽而拂拭之，則塵垢不止，而妍媸常定矣；水欲其常清，時其未淆而正錯之，則湛濁不動，足以燭鬚眉而察理矣。君心之天，其初而欲之未萌也，虛然明耳，湛然清耳。當是之時，有理無欲，有天無人；完其理，守其天，而不以人欲參焉，其爲防甚易也。然而理與欲迭爲貞勝，天與人迭爲消長；故出乎理則入乎欲，人爲主則天必漓。自此則牽引蔓延，潰裂四出，而始難防矣。非防之難，其防於已萌者之難也。若夫未萌之防，則人主之所以易其防也，是衆人以爲不必防，而君子深以爲當防者也。知其當防，及其初而豫爲之
translation_en: …even if he is fortunate enough to see it clearly in his mind, he will not necessarily guard against it right away; even if he guards against it, he will not necessarily be able to recover right away; and even if he recovers, before that recovery takes place, the harm done cannot be fathomed and cannot be undone. That guarding against desires after they have already sprouted has such an outcome is the fault of not taking precautions at the beginning; it is a matter of recovering one's original heavenly nature rather than preserving one's original heavenly nature. Therefore, one who is skilled at guarding against desires should not guard against them after they have already sprouted, but should guard against them before they have sprouted. Now, the state before desires have sprouted is the original heavenly nature, the initial state of the mind—is it not like the brightness of a mirror and the clarity of water? If one wishes a mirror to be ever bright, and wipes it while it is not yet obscured, then dust and grime will not settle upon it, and beauty and ugliness will always be clearly distinguished. If one wishes water to be ever clear, and keeps it still and undisturbed while it is not yet muddied, then sunken dregs will not be stirred up, and it will suffice to reflect beard and eyebrows and to discern fine patterns. As for the heavenly nature of the ruler's mind, in its initial state before desires have sprouted, it is simply vacuously bright and limpidly clear. At such a time, there is principle without desire, Heaven without the human; to keep its principle intact, to guard its heavenly nature, and not to let human desires intrude therein—such prevention is very easy. Yet principle and desire alternately prevail over one another, and Heaven and the human alternately wax and wane; thus, to depart from principle is to enter into desire, and when the human becomes master, the heavenly nature inevitably erodes. From this point on, desires draw one another along and spread, bursting forth in all directions, and only then do they become difficult to guard against. It is not that guarding against them is inherently difficult, but that guarding against them after they have already sprouted is difficult. As for guarding against them before they have sprouted, that is whereby the ruler makes his prevention easy; this is what the multitude consider unnecessary to guard against, whereas the gentleman deeply considers it imperative to guard against. Knowing that it must be guarded against, and taking precautions against it while it is still in its initial state…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
防視無若有視未形以爲已形故用力省而取
效博也是故守真保素謹於冲夷恬淡之時却
照返觀嚴於凝寂定靜之際戒謹恐懼凜於尸
居淵默之境憂勤祗惕勵於蚤夜平旦之候聲
色未邇也而燕處雅頌居寢瞽御慎防其淫玩
好未開也而異物不貴遠物不寶慎防其侈未
懷宴安而日出聽政日昃不遑防佚豫也未思
馳騁而遊田有箴蒐狩有禮防荒樂也土木未
興而有勞民費財之防是故瓊瑶示戒雕峻示
===
警焉邊功未啓而有起釁召禍之防是故却贄
不享閉關謝使焉虞賓在位三恪助祭夏士在
庭殷士在廟讎民在甸夷隸在門防吾之萌于
欲也疑丞後先卜筮左右太史奉諱工師誦詩
御瞽幾聲士庶傳謗防人之萌吾欲也夫是謂
禁於未發夫是謂保於無躬若是者豈故用其
心於無所用之地而爲是私憂過計哉其防於
未萌者正所以絕其已萌者也蓋至是則理常
爲主欲常爲客人泯而本然之天常如其初矣
punctuated: 防，視無若有，視未形以爲已形，故用力省而取效博也。是故守真保素，謹於冲夷恬淡之時；却照返觀，嚴於凝寂定靜之際；戒謹恐懼，凜於尸居淵默之境；憂勤祗惕，勵於蚤夜平旦之候。聲色未邇也，而燕處雅頌、居寢瞽御，慎防其淫；玩好未開也，而異物不貴、遠物不寶，慎防其侈。未懷宴安，而日出聽政、日昃不遑，防佚豫也；未思馳騁，而遊田有箴、蒐狩有禮，防荒樂也。土木未興，而有勞民費財之防，是故瓊瑶示戒、雕峻示警焉；邊功未啓，而有起釁召禍之防，是故却贄不享、閉關謝使焉。虞賓在位，三恪助祭，夏士在庭，殷士在廟，讎民在甸，夷隸在門，防吾之萌于欲也；疑丞後先，卜筮左右，太史奉諱，工師誦詩，御瞽幾聲，士庶傳謗，防人之萌吾欲也。夫是謂禁於未發，夫是謂保於無躬。若是者，豈故用其心於無所用之地，而爲是私憂過計哉？其防於未萌者，正所以絕其已萌者也。蓋至是則理常爲主，欲常爲客，人泯而本然之天常如其初矣。
translation_en: …prevention, regarding what does not yet exist as though it did, and treating what is still formless as though it had already taken form; therefore, the effort expended is slight while the results achieved are vast. Thus, in guarding his genuineness and preserving his simplicity, he is cautious during moments of calm and tranquil detachment; in turning his gaze inward for self-reflection, he is strict amidst stillness and settled composure; in being wary and fearful, he stands in awe in a state of motionless, abyssal silence; in being anxious, diligent, respectful, and vigilant, he exerts himself from early morning to late night and at the break of dawn. Sensual pleasures of music and beauty have not yet drawn near, yet in leisure he listens to the Odes and Hymns and in his bedchamber he is attended by blind musicians, carefully guarding against licentiousness; a taste for curiosities and playthings has not yet begun, yet he does not value strange objects or treasure things from afar, carefully guarding against extravagance. Before harboring thoughts of ease and comfort, he hears affairs of state at sunrise and allows himself no leisure until the sun slants west, guarding against idleness and indulgence; before thinking of galloping abroad, he has admonitions on excursions and hunting and ritual rules for spring and winter hunts, guarding against wild pleasures. Before construction projects are launched, he takes precautions against exhausting the people and wasting wealth, and therefore displays warnings against jade-adorned halls and lofty carved palaces; before frontier campaigns are opened, he takes precautions against provoking hostilities and inviting disaster, and therefore rejects tribute gifts without accepting them as offerings and closes the passes to turn away envoys. The guests from Yu are in their places, the descendants of the three former dynasties assist at the sacrifices, the officers of Xia are in the courtyard, the officers of Yin are in the ancestral temple, the recalcitrant people are in the royal domain, and the barbarian bondservants are at the gates—all to guard against desires sprouting within himself; the grand mentors and assistants attend before and behind, the diviners by tortoise-shell and milfoil stand to the left and right, the Grand Scribe presents warnings on tabooed conduct, the master artisans recite poems, the attending blind musicians examine the musical tones, and the officers and commoners pass along criticisms—all to guard against others causing desires to sprout within him. This is what is meant by prohibiting evil before it manifests; this is what is meant by preserving oneself before trouble takes form [?]. In acting thus, is he deliberately applying his mind where it has no use and engaging in private worries and excessive calculations? Guarding against what has not yet sprouted is precisely the means to cut off what has already sprouted. Indeed, when this point is reached, principle is always the master and desire is always the guest; human artifice vanishes, and the original nature of Heaven remains ever as it was in the beginning.

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
是故虛然常明湛然常清性靜情恬神凝氣定
而妄思雜慮無所留也即其怡心適志之事日
交於前而隨過隨滅弗能擾也巧言勿聽諛說
勿容而震撼揺動弗能傾也尚何欲之能萌而
亦奚難於防哉何也彼其初固防之豫也豫故
不難也而成效所臻能使庶績凝百度貞德化
薰蒸蒼生康豫普天率土無呻吟咨籲之聲而
常有忻懽鼓舞之志相愉以樂相恬以熙相安
於太平無事之天而莫知誰氏之賜此防於未
===
萌之明驗也蓋古之善防者莫若周成王其詩
曰日就月將學有緝熙于光明曰光明者欲未
萌之初此心本然之天也曰就曰將曰緝熙無
時而不豫為之防也故成王之學至于基命宥
密克單厥心而四方日靖與二后比隆此善保
其初者也後世若漢武帝之悔輪臺唐太宗之
悔遼左感悼懲創惕然思幡然悟毅然而隨以
止非不稱知防也然而君子不滿焉以其能防
已萌而不知防未萌也是失之初而救於終汩
punctuated: 是故虛然常明，湛然常清，性靜情恬，神凝氣定，而妄思雜慮無所留也。即其怡心適志之事日交於前，而隨過隨滅，弗能擾也；巧言勿聽，諛說勿容，而震撼揺動弗能傾也。尚何欲之能萌，而亦奚難於防哉？何也？彼其初固防之豫也，豫故不難也。而成效所臻，能使庶績凝，百度貞，德化薰蒸，蒼生康豫。普天率土無呻吟咨籲之聲，而常有忻懽鼓舞之志，相愉以樂，相恬以熙，相安於太平無事之天，而莫知誰氏之賜。此防於未萌之明驗也。蓋古之善防者，莫若周成王。其詩曰：「日就月將，學有緝熙于光明。」曰「光明」者，欲未萌之初，此心本然之天也；曰「就」、曰「將」、曰「緝熙」，無時而不豫為之防也。故成王之學，至于「基命宥密，克單厥心」，而四方日靖，與二后比隆，此善保其初者也。後世若漢武帝之悔輪臺，唐太宗之悔遼左，感悼懲創，惕然思，幡然悟，毅然而隨以止，非不稱知防也。然而君子不滿焉，以其能防已萌，而不知防未萌也。是失之初而救於終，汩
translation_en: Therefore, the mind remains vacuously ever-luminous and limpidly ever-clear; one's nature is tranquil and emotions calm, one's spirit concentrated and vital breath settled, so that deluded thoughts and miscellaneous anxieties have nowhere to linger. Even when things that delight the heart and gratify the will pass before one daily, they vanish as soon as they pass and cannot disturb one; artful words are not heeded and flattering talk is not tolerated, so that shocks and tremors cannot overturn one. What desires could still sprout, and what difficulty would there be in guarding against them? Why is this? Because in the beginning, one indeed guarded against them beforehand; because it was done beforehand, it is not difficult. And the results achieved can cause the myriad accomplishments to be consolidated, the hundred standards of conduct to be rectified, moral transformation to permeate like rising vapor, and the common people to enjoy peace and comfort. Under the whole heaven and to the borders of the land, there are no sounds of groaning or crying out in distress, while there is ever a spirit of joy and elation; people delight together in happiness, rest together in harmony, and dwell together in peace under a heaven of great tranquility and eventlessness, without knowing whose gift it is. This is the clear proof of guarding against desires before they sprout. Indeed, among those in antiquity who were good at guarding against desires, none surpassed King Cheng of Zhou 周成王. His ode says: "With daily progress and monthly advance, I learn so that there is continuous brightness toward illumination." What is called "illumination" is the original heaven of this mind in the beginning before desires have sprouted; what are called "progress," "advance," and "continuous brightness" mean that there is no time when one is not taking precautions to guard against them beforehand. Thus King Cheng's learning reached the point of "establishing the Mandate in breadth and stillness, able to exhaust his heart," so that the four quarters grew daily more tranquil and his rule rivaled the grandeur of the Two Sovereigns (Wen and Wu); this was someone who knew well how to preserve his initial state. In later ages, cases such as Emperor Wu of Han's 漢武帝 regret over Luntai 輪臺 and Emperor Taizong of Tang's 唐太宗 regret over Liaozuo 遼左—where they felt grief and chastened themselves, reflected in alarm, awakened suddenly, and resolutely brought things to a halt—cannot be said not to have known how to guard against desires. Yet the gentleman is dissatisfied with them, because they were able to guard against what had already sprouted, but did not know how to guard against what had not yet sprouted. This is losing it at the beginning and rescuing it at the end, submerging…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
於人而後復其天者也故其力弗豫而其功難
圖也故海內未秏輪臺之詔未肯下也遼俘果
獻班師之詔未可期也蓋萌成也一成而不肯
變故難防也然則人主奚防哉防於未萌而已
矣抑防又有要焉烏喙之毒也神農氏辨之揭
書以詔後世自古及今未有中其毒者之燕者
南行向于郢或告之曰此非適燕之路也遂反
焉故往哲遺言今世之明鑑也逆耳忠告岐路
之指南也今夫嗜欲之戕人不啻烏喙矣而古
===
訓備之理欲之殊塗不啻燕郢矣而明者能別
之然則人主欲防未萌之欲者其惟學古乎其
惟親賢乎善乎真德秀有言曰惟學可以養此
心惟賢人君子可以維持此心此防未萌之要
法也此又程氏未盡之旨也
表
擬宋御製爲君難爲臣不易論示輔臣謝
表〔祥符五年〕
陳堯言
punctuated:
於人而後復其天者也，故其力弗豫而其功難圖也。故海內未秏，輪臺之詔未肯下也；遼俘果獻，班師之詔未可期也。蓋萌成也，一成而不肯變，故難防也。然則人主奚防哉？防於未萌而已矣。抑防又有要焉。烏喙之毒也，神農氏辨之，揭書以詔後世，自古及今，未有中其毒者；之燕者南行向于郢，或告之曰：「此非適燕之路也。」遂反焉。故往哲遺言，今世之明鑑也；逆耳忠告，岐路之指南也。今夫嗜欲之戕人，不啻烏喙矣，而古訓備之；理欲之殊塗，不啻燕郢矣，而明者能別之。然則人主欲防未萌之欲者，其惟學古乎！其惟親賢乎！善乎真德秀有言曰：「惟學可以養此心，惟賢人君子可以維持此心。」此防未萌之要法也，此又程氏未盡之旨也。

表
擬宋御製《爲君難爲臣不易論》示輔臣謝表〔祥符五年〕
陳堯言
translation_en:
…by human desires before recovering its heavenly nature; therefore their effort was not made beforehand and their success was hard to achieve. Thus, had the realm within the seas not yet been exhausted, the edict of Luntai would not yet have been willingly issued; had captives from Liaodong indeed been presented, the edict to withdraw the army could not yet have been expected. For once the sprout has grown, once formed it refuses to change, and therefore is hard to guard against. How, then, should a ruler guard against desires? Simply by guarding against them before they sprout.

Moreover, there are essentials to such guarding. As for the poison of aconite (wuhui), the Divine Husbandman (Shennong) identified it and posted writings to instruct later generations, so from antiquity to the present no one has been poisoned by it. When someone going to Yan traveled south toward Ying, someone told him, "This is not the road to Yan," and he thereupon turned back. Therefore, the words left by past sages are a clear mirror for the present age, and loyal advice that grates on the ear is a compass at the crossroads. Now the way indulgence and desire harm people is more than that of aconite, and ancient teachings have provided completely against it; the divergence of paths between heavenly principle and human desire is greater than that between Yan and Ying, and the clear-sighted are able to distinguish them. Thus, if a ruler wishes to guard against desires before they sprout, should it not be solely through studying antiquity? Should it not be solely through drawing close to the worthy? Well indeed did Zhen Dexiu 真德秀 say: "Only learning can nourish this mind; only worthy men and gentlemen can sustain this mind." This is the essential method for guarding against desires before they sprout, and this too is the import that Master Cheng (Cheng Yi 程頤) left unexhausted.

Memorial (biao)
An Imitation of a Song-Dynasty Memorial of Gratitude upon the Emperor's Showing His Imperially Composed "Discourse on the Difficulty of Being a Ruler and the Uneasiness of Being a Minister" to the Assisting Wolverhampton Officials [5th year of the Xiangfu era (1012)]
Chen Yaoyan 陳堯言

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
同考試官敎諭田批構意造語多合雅調非尋
常手筆可到
同考試官敎諭畢批作此者類多勦襲舊語是
作不特剪裁亦見忠愛之悃
考試官敎諭林批詞工意懇可錄
考試官敎諭吳批典麗
祥符五年某月某日伏蒙
聖恩示臣等
御製爲君難爲臣不易論謹上
===
表稱
謝者伏以
道協二儀羲象發地天之祕
聖隆一德堯文宣日月之華
晉錫鼎衡
泰交堂陛奉
奎章而拜手載
舜訓以銘心臣某等誠惶誠恐稽首頓首上言
竊惟帝乃神聖武文幾猶嚴乎慎位臣作
punctuated:
同考試官敎諭田批：構意造語，多合雅調，非尋常手筆可到。
同考試官敎諭畢批：作此者類多勦襲舊語，是作不特剪裁，亦見忠愛之悃。
考試官敎諭林批：詞工意懇，可錄。
考試官敎諭吳批：典麗。
祥符五年某月某日，伏蒙聖恩示臣等《御製爲君難爲臣不易論》，謹上表稱謝者。伏以道協二儀，羲象發地天之祕；聖隆一德，堯文宣日月之華。晉錫鼎衡，泰交堂陛。奉奎章而拜手，載舜訓以銘心。臣某等誠惶誠恐，稽首頓首上言：竊惟帝乃神聖武文，幾猶嚴乎慎位；臣作
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Tian comments: The conception of ideas and phrasing of expressions largely conform to an elegant tone; it is not something an ordinary hand could achieve.
Associate Examiner and County Director of Studies Bi comments: Those who compose on this topic mostly plagiarize old phrases; this piece not only shows skillful tailoring, it also reveals a sincere spirit of loyalty and devotion.
Examiner and County Director of Studies Lin comments: The wording is skillful and the meaning earnest; worthy of recording.
Examiner and County Director of Studies Wu comments: Classical and ornate.
On a certain day of a certain month in the fifth year of the Xiangfu era [1012], having humbly received the imperial grace of showing Your servants the Imperially Composed Discourse on "Being a Ruler Is Difficult, Being a Minister Is Not Easy" (Yuzhi weijun nan weichen buyi lun), we reverently submit this memorial to express our gratitude.
We humbly reflect that as the Way harmonizes with the Two Primal Forces, the hexagrams of Fuxi reveal the mysteries of earth and heaven; as sageliness exalts the One Virtue, the literary brilliance of Yao proclaims the splendor of the sun and moon. Abundant gifts are bestowed upon the chief ministers, and harmonious communion joins the throne and its steps. Receiving the imperial composition, we bow with clasped hands; bearing the instructions of Shun, we engrave them upon our hearts.
Your servants so-and-so and others, in utmost fear and trepidation, bow our heads to the ground and reverently state: We humbly consider that though the Emperor is神聖 [divine and sage], martial and civil, in the subtle springs of action he is still strict about being cautious in his position; the ministers act as…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
股肱耳目義必重於欽鄰故垂衣聽朝誥
興若采錫圭祗奏謨矢克艱歌勅明良虞
后絲綸駿發命休乂食商宗黼藻鴻宣湯
陟丕釐瞻九主而嚴三宅成基宥密鑒四
牖以翼十夫惟作聖述明用軫無虞之戒
故君仁臣直咸綿有道之長肆喜起之聲
希越諂驕之響應端居寶曆情罔繫乎苞
桑望重金鉉慮弗廑於覆餗箴規日隔駕
言魚水之懽倡和雷同寧作鷰堂之處集
===
柏梁而歌詠徒矜一豫一遊宴凌煙以品
題孰誠同心同德
聖明天啓輔弼雲從玆蓋伏遇
〇〇〇〇
德合乾坤
文行風水
芝封玉檢
王心允眷於
天心
punctuated: 股肱耳目，義必重於欽鄰。故垂衣聽朝，誥興若采；錫圭祗奏，謨矢克艱。歌勅明良，虞后絲綸駿發；命休乂食，商宗黼藻鴻宣。湯陟丕釐，瞻九主而嚴三宅；成基宥密，鑒四牖以翼十夫。惟作聖述明，用軫無虞之戒；故君仁臣直，咸綿有道之長。肆喜起之聲希，越諂驕之響應。端居寶曆，情罔繫乎苞桑；望重金鉉，慮弗廑於覆餗。箴規日隔，駕言魚水之懽；倡和雷同，寧作鷰堂之處？集柏梁而歌詠，徒矜一豫一遊；宴凌煙以品題，孰誠同心同德？聖明天啓，輔弼雲從。玆蓋伏遇〇〇〇〇，德合乾坤，文行風水。芝封玉檢，王心允眷於天心；
translation_en:
… limbs and his eyes and ears, in righteousness they must place weight on reverently assisting the sovereign. Thus, when the sovereign let his robes hang down and held audience at court, his announcements arose to seek out those suited to their tasks; when the minister was bestowed the jade tablet and respectfully submitted his reports, his counsels pledged to overcome the difficulties of office. Composing the song admonishing enlightened ruler and worthy ministers, the Yu sovereign swiftly issued his silken decrees; charging his minister to season the royal food nicely, the Shang ancestor grandly proclaimed his embroidered words. When Tang ascended to bring about great order, one looked to the nine types of rulers and strictly observed the three appointments of the worthy; when King Cheng laid his foundation in quietude and profundity, one looked to the four windows and assisted with the ten able men. Only because a sage creates and an enlightened one transmits did they take to heart the warning against being unprepared for danger; therefore, with the ruler benevolent and the ministers upright, they all prolonged the enduring reign of the Way.

Yet once the songs of "rejoicing and rising" grew rare, the echoes of flattery and arrogance responded in turn. Sitting upright in possession of the precious calendar of the throne, their sentiments were not bound to the sturdy mulberry roots; holding high prestige as the golden tripod-rings of state, their thoughts were not anxiously concerned with overturning the tripod's stew. As admonitions and remonstrances grew daily more distant, they falsely spoke of the joy of fish and water; echoing one another in blind conformity, how was that any different from swallows dwelling in a hall awaiting fire? Gathering at the Cypress-Beam Terrace to compose songs, they merely boasted of a single excursion or amusement; feasting at the Lingyan Pavilion to bestow appreciative inscriptions, who among them was truly of one heart and one virtue?

When sacred enlightenment is opened by Heaven, assisting ministers follow like clouds. Now, we humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], whose virtue matches Heaven and Earth, and whose literary grace moves like wind over water. With ganoderma seals and jade-inscribed slips, the King's heart truly cleaves to Heaven's heart; …

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
藻思瑶編
君道率先乎臣道欹器有
賛仰
龍德之正中崇術敷言識
鴻猷之廣大邇於
萬幾之暇永念一言之艱謂
九重繫四海之安危豈容逸豫而百僚共
一人之休戚寧事逢迎誕啓
玄精親揮
===
宸翰紬繹乎無怠無荒之旨反覆乎多譽多懼
之占敘感遇而興思氷淵咸惕勉正直以
行事蓍蔡永懷
先后謨謀廣著
席前之問累朝得失罄繙
座右之藏
帝典
皇猷禹皐服之無斁
金聲玉振游夏賛而莫能
punctuated: 藻思瑶編，君道率先乎臣道。欹器有賛，仰龍德之正中；崇術敷言，識鴻猷之廣大。邇於萬幾之暇，永念一言之艱。謂九重繫四海之安危，豈容逸豫；而百僚共一人之休戚，寧事逢迎。誕啓玄精，親揮宸翰。紬繹乎「無怠無荒」之旨，反覆乎「多譽多懼」之占。敘感遇而興思，氷淵咸惕；勉正直以行事，蓍蔡永懷。先后謨謀，廣著席前之問；累朝得失，罄繙座右之藏。帝典皇猷，禹、皐服之無斁；金聲玉振，游、夏賛而莫能。
translation_en: …and in refined thoughts and jade-like compilations, the Way of the Ruler takes precedence in leading the Way of the Minister. When the tilting vessel received a eulogy, we looked up to the rectitude and centrality of Your Dragon Virtue; when lofty arts were expounded in words, we recognized the vastness and greatness of Your Grand Plan. Recently, in Your leisure from the myriad affairs of state, You have perpetually reflected on the difficulty of a single word. You have declared that the Ninefold Palace is bound to the security and peril of the Four Seas—how could comfort and idleness be permitted?—and that the hundred officials share the joys and sorrows of the One Man—how could they engage in flattery and pandering? Thus You grandly opened Your profound mind and personally wielded the imperial brush. You drew out and expounded the import of "without negligence, without荒 [abandon/excess]," and repeatedly pondered the prognostication of "much praise and much fear." Recounting the appreciation of Your encounter with your ministers to inspire reflection, all tread as if on thin ice or by a deep abyss in shared vigilance; exhorting uprightness and rectitude in the conduct of affairs, such counsel is forever cherished like milfoil and tortoise-shell divination. The plans and counsels of former sovereigns are broadly set forth in inquiries before the imperial mat; the successes and failures of successive reigns are exhaustively unrolled from the collections beside the throne. To such Imperial Canons and August Plans, Yu 禹 and Gao Yao 皐陶 would submit without ever tiring; before such golden sound and jade vibration, Ziyou 子游 and Zixia 子夏 could not offer a single word of praise. …

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
詔發西崑製恢唐體
文躔東壁雅邁漢風展
寶卷於
黼扆首頒芸閣横牙籤於
籞禁副載蘭臺眷茲
上下之交奚啻腹心之感臣等俯慙石畫仰荷
珍符誦
帝德之罔愆莫裨高厚代天工之無曠未效涓
埃拜
===
錫百朋色動青藜之影捧聯什襲光生
紫泥之封敢不刻以丹衷期遠垂乎竹帛佩
玆素志謝近取於韋弦致
君深戒面從論事何妨骨鯁蹇王臣而附鳳舉
矢竭微忠歌天保以報鹿鳴益祈
戩穀遵
德音於補袞悟
雅意於忘筌伏願
君君臣臣兢兢業業
punctuated: 詔發西崑，製恢唐體；文躔東壁，雅邁漢風。展寶卷於黼扆，首頒芸閣；横牙籤於籞禁，副載蘭臺。眷茲上下之交，奚啻腹心之感！臣等俯慙石畫，仰荷珍符。誦帝德之罔愆，莫裨高厚；代天工之無曠，未效涓埃。拜錫百朋，色動青藜之影；捧聯什襲，光生紫泥之封。敢不刻以丹衷，期遠垂乎竹帛；佩玆素志，謝近取於韋弦。致君深戒面從，論事何妨骨鯁。蹇王臣而附鳳舉，矢竭微忠；歌《天保》以報《鹿鳴》，益祈戩穀。遵德音於補袞，悟雅意於忘筌。伏願君君臣臣，兢兢業業，
translation_en: The edicts issued from the Western Kunlun expand upon the Tang style in their composition; the literary brilliance residing in the Eastern Wall constellation surpasses the Han manner in its elegance. Unrolling the precious scrolls before the embroidered screen, they are first bestowed upon the Rue Pavilion; laying across the ivory book-tags in the Imperial Precincts, duplicate copies are stored in the Orchid Terrace. Looking upon this communion of ruler above and ministers below, how is it merely a feeling of gratitude in our hearts and minds! Your servants bow in shame over our lack of rock-solid plans, while looking up to receive this precious talisman of favor. Reciting how the Imperial virtue is free of fault, we cannot add to Your height and thickness; acting on behalf of Heaven's work without neglect, we have not contributed even a drop of water or a speck of dust. Bowing to receive the gift of a hundred sets of cowries, our faces are moved by the glow of the green藜-staff lamp; holding the volumes wrapped in tenfold layers, radiance springs from the purple-clay seal. How dare we not engrave them upon our loyal hearts, hoping to hand our names down far into the future on bamboo and silk; wearing this pure resolve at our girdles, we have no need of drawing near to the leather strap and bowstring for self-correction. In serving our Sovereign, we deeply guard against mere outward compliance; in discussing affairs of state, what harm is there in outspoken candor? Toiling as the King's ministers and clinging to the phoenix's flight, we swear to exhaust our humble loyalty; singing "Heaven Protects" (Tianbao) in response to "The Deer Calls" (Luming), we pray all the more for Your perfection and blessing. Following Your virtuous voice to mend the royal robes, we comprehend Your refined meaning to the point of forgetting the fish-trap once the fish is caught. We humbly wish that ruler be ruler and minister be minister, cautious and industrious,…

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
臨民若馭朽敬懷可願之脩
從諫如轉圜懋延交儆之益禹湯文武媲千
古而凝
配帝之圖稷契伊周聚一堂而建
格天之治臣等無任瞻
天仰
聖激切屏營之至謹奉
表稱
謝以
===
聞
第叄場
策
第一問
王建中
同考試官敎諭陳批仁孝立說足以仰誦
聖天子格天錫極之蘊而援據明實可錄
同考試官敎諭黃批敷陳合祀養老之議甚爲
明悉宜錄以式
punctuated:
臨民若馭朽，敬懷可願之脩；從諫如轉圜，懋延交儆之益。禹、湯、文、武媲千古而凝配帝之圖，稷、契、伊、周聚一堂而建格天之治。臣等無任瞻天仰聖，激切屏營之至，謹奉表稱謝以聞。

第叄場
策
第一問
王建中
同考試官敎諭陳批：「仁孝立說，足以仰誦聖天子格天錫極之蘊，而援據明實，可錄。」
同考試官敎諭黃批：「敷陳合祀養老之議，甚爲明悉，宜錄以式。」
translation_en:
…approach the people as if driving with rotten reins, reverently cherishing the cultivation of what is desirable; and follow remonstrance as smoothly as turning a circle, earnestly extending the benefit of mutual admonition. Then Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu will be matched across a thousand ages to consolidate a plan worthy of being paired with the Supreme Lord; and Hou Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, and the Duke of Zhou will gather in one hall to establish a governance that reaches Heaven. Your servants, unable to contain the utmost earnestness and trepidation as we gaze up at Heaven and look up to Your Sacred Majesty, reverently present this memorial of gratitude for Your Majesty's hearing.

Third Session
Policy Essays
First Question
Wang Jianzhong (王建中)
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Chen: "Developing his argument on the basis of benevolence and filial piety, he suffices to reverently extol the profound meaning of the Sacred Son of Heaven reaching Heaven and bestowing the highest standard; furthermore, his citations and evidence are clear and substantive. Worthy of selection."
Comment by Associate Examiner and Instructor Huang: "His exposition of the discussions on joint sacrifices and nourishing the elderly is exceedingly clear and thorough. It ought to be selected as a model."

title: 萬曆四年浙江鄉試錄
text:
考試官敎諭林批〔敷答詳明引據切當〕
考試官敎諭吳批〔援禮議制卓然有見〕
帝王之會作述而垂典禮也有格天之至
仁而昭事於不匱有法聖之達孝而錫極
於無方夫禮有本也有文也而考禮者貴
繹其義行禮者貴返諸古是故王者爲天
元子於是有升中饗帝之禮焉無非所以
達類禋之馨德迓眷顧之顯休也抑豈徒
以肅雖陟降爲哉是必有精通天地者相
===
疑會焉而合祀之議則凝之之大端也作
民君師於是有釋奠臨雍之禮焉無非所
以示尊聖之謙光廣崇儒之弘德也抑豈
徒以屈體侈觀已哉是必有孝治天下者
相風勸焉而養老之議則風之之大要也
然禮有屢更於制作而習於因者憚變易
之難禮有常行於曠古而廢於久者詘脩
復之迂方今
聖天子格天之德懋敬於
punctuated:
考試官敎諭林批：〔敷答詳明，引據切當。〕
考試官敎諭吳批：〔援禮議制，卓然有見。〕

帝王之會作述而垂典禮也，有格天之至仁，而昭事於不匱；有法聖之達孝，而錫極於無方。夫禮有本也，有文也，而考禮者貴繹其義，行禮者貴返諸古。是故王者爲天元子，於是有升中饗帝之禮焉，無非所以達類禋之馨德，迓眷顧之顯休也。抑豈徒以肅雖陟降爲哉？是必有精通天地者相疑會焉，而合祀之議則凝之之大端也。作民君師，於是有釋奠臨雍之禮焉，無非所以示尊聖之謙光，廣崇儒之弘德也。抑豈徒以屈體侈觀已哉？是必有孝治天下者相風勸焉，而養老之議則風之之大要也。然禮有屢更於制作，而習於因者憚變易之難；禮有常行於曠古，而廢於久者詘脩復之迂。方今聖天子格天之德，懋敬於
translation_en:
Examiner and Instructor Lin comments: [The exposition in the answer is detailed and clear, and the citations of evidence are apt and fitting.]
Examiner and Instructor Wu comments: [Drawing upon the rites to deliberate on institutions, it shows outstanding insight.]

When emperors and kings bring together creation and transmission to hand down canonical rites, they possess the utmost benevolence that reaches Heaven, thus serving it brightly without fail; and they possess the far-reaching filial piety that models itself on the sages, thus bestowing the standard of perfection without bounds. Now, rites have their root and their outward form; those who examine the rites value unraveling their meaning, while those who practice the rites value returning to antiquity. Therefore, the true king is the Eldest Son of Heaven, and thus there is the rite of offering the burnt sacrifice at the zenith and feasting the Supreme Ancestor. This is nothing other than the means to convey the fragrant virtue of the special and pure sacrifices, and to welcome the manifest blessings of Heaven's favor. Yet how could this merely be a matter of solemn harmony [?] in ascending and descending? There must surely be a spirit that penetrates Heaven and Earth coalescing [?] therein, and the deliberation on joint sacrifice is the great principle for coalescing it. He acts as ruler and teacher to the people, and thus there are the rites of offering libations to the sages and visiting the Imperial Academy. This is nothing other than the means to display the humble radiance of honoring the sages, and to broaden the vast virtue of revering Confucianism. Yet how could this merely end with bending one's posture to make a lavish spectacle? There must surely be a filial governance of the world inspiring and encouraging therein, and the deliberation on nourishing the aged is the great essential for inspiring it. However, when rites have been repeatedly altered in their institutionalization, those accustomed to following precedent dread the difficulty of change; and when rites were regularly practiced in remote antiquity, those who have let them lapse for a long time dismiss their restoration as impractical.
